passage: Joseph, 24, leans into the community-radio microphone. 'You asked who I look up to. Honestly? Uma Aunty, our choir leader. She's seventy-one. Last Christmas she taught the wrong harmony for a whole week, and when the youngest singer pointed it out, she stopped, laughed and said, "You're right, I've been leading you all into a ditch." Then she asked the kid to show everyone. She asks us younger ones what songs we want. She listens even when we're half-joking. Compare that with the committee member who shouts "Respect your elders!" at us. We nod at him and roll our eyes once he's gone. For Uma Aunty, nobody has to be told. We just stand up when she walks in.'

qa.q: What does Joseph feel towards Uma Aunty, and why?
qa.a: Joseph feels deep admiration and warmth, because she admits her mistakes, asks the younger singers' opinions and truly listens.

qa.q: What could the committee member learn from Uma Aunty?
qa.a: That respect comes from listening and owning mistakes, not from demanding it; shouting only earns eye-rolls behind his back.

qa.q: How might the youngest singer have felt when Uma Aunty admitted the mistake?
qa.a: The singer probably felt proud and valued, since speaking up was welcomed and even turned into a chance to lead.

grounding: Shows a junior who watches an elder admit errors, ask opinions and listen, and gives that elder real respect unasked, while demanded respect earns only hidden eye-rolling.

passage:
From my desk opposite the chief sub-editor's, I've watched Harish-da for eight months. He's fifty-eight and has been at the paper longer than I've been alive. Yesterday a trainee pointed out that his headline had the wrong district name. The room went silent. Harish-da took off his glasses, read it again, and said, 'Good catch. Fix it, and put your initials on it.' At the Monday meeting he asks the youngest reporters first which stories matter, then listens with his chin on his hand. I can't tell what he's thinking behind that calm face. I just know that when he walks in, we all sit up, and nobody ever told us to.
Anirban

qa.q: What did Harish-da tell the trainee to do?
qa.a: 'Fix it, and put your initials on it.'

qa.q: What does Anirban feel towards Harish-da, and what shows it?
qa.a: Anirban feels admiration and respect, shown by sitting up when Harish-da walks in without ever being told to.

qa.q: What could a new senior learn from how Harish-da handled the wrong district name?
qa.a: To admit the error calmly and credit the person who caught it; that earns lasting respect instead of fear.

qa.q: Why might Harish-da choose to ask the youngest reporters first?
qa.a: He may believe fresh eyes see what he misses and want them to know their views count, though Anirban can only guess his thoughts.

grounding: Illustrates a junior colleague watching an elder who admits mistakes, asks the young for opinions and listens, and giving that elder real respect without being told.
